lessons.title: Which way do you lean? 16 cards, no wrong answers
lessons.body:
1 · Hook

Most students pick a stream the way they pick a cricket team: because everyone around them did. Then they spend Class 11 wondering why it feels wrong.

This week and next, you will try real Class 11 work from all four streams. But first, a quick read of your instincts. It takes five minutes and feeds your Stream Report at the end of week 2.

2 · Play

Sixteen cards. Each one is a sentence about you. Tap That's me or Not me. Go fast; your first instinct is the honest one.

[[widget:cards]]

3 · Name it

The four bars are the four streams: PCM (physics, chemistry, maths: engineering, architecture, data), PCB (biology: medicine, research, life sciences), Commerce (accounts, business, economics: CA, finance, management) and Humanities (history, political science, psychology, languages: law, civil services, writing, design).

Your bars show where your interests leaned today. Interest is one input. Over the next ten days you will add the other three: how the taster lessons feel, a diagnostic test, and your own reflections. The report at the end of week 2 puts all four together.

4 · Do it

Nothing to grade here. Three honest questions below, saved for your mentor.

5 · AI twist

Open ChatGPT, Gemini or Claude and ask: "Which stream should I pick after Class 10?" Notice what it does: it asks you questions back, or it gives a generic answer. It cannot know you. Neither can this card deck alone. That is why the report uses four inputs and a person reads it before it reaches you.

questions.q: If you had a free Saturday and no phone, which would you most likely do?
options: Fix, build or take apart something
Watch or read about nature, bodies, medicine
Write, draw, debate or read a story

questions.q: Which of these do your parents expect, honestly?
And which would you pick if nobody else had a say?

lessons.title: Why does double the speed give four times the height?
lessons.body:
1 · Hook

A cricketer throws a ball straight up at 15 m/s. It reaches about 11 metres. Her friend throws at 30 m/s, exactly double. How high does his go? Most people say 22 m. The real answer is 45 m. Not double. Four times.

Why? Don't read ahead. Find out below by throwing balls yourself.

2 · Play

Pick a speed, type your guess for the height first, then throw. Do it at least three times with very different speeds. Wrong guesses are the whole point; that's how your brain notices the pattern.

[[widget:ball-throw]]

3 · Name it

Watch the four scenes. Abhi narrates if Listen is on.

[[widget:explainer:kinematics]]

What you just found has a name. When something is thrown straight up with speed u and gravity pulls it down at g (about 10 m/s² on Earth):

height = u² ÷ 2g   ·   time in the air = 2u ÷ g

Check it against your table: 20 m/s gives 400 ÷ 20 = 20 m and 4 s. The u² is why doubling the speed quadruples the height. That's the only new thing in Class 11 kinematics: in Class 10 you plugged into formulas; in Class 11 you're expected to know why the formula has that shape. You now do.

Where it comes from, if you're curious: at the top the ball's speed is zero. Using v² = u² + 2as with v = 0 and a = −g gives s = u²/2g. Same equation you had in Class 10, just used with a sign.

4 · Do it

Four questions below. Use the hints. Every one is a thing you just saw happen.

5 · AI twist

Open ChatGPT, Gemini or Claude and ask: "If I throw a ball up at 30 m/s, how high does it go? Explain like I'm 15."

Now check it against your table and the formula. Did it get 45 m? Did it explain the square? Did it say anything you can prove wrong with your own throws? Write one line about it in your diary at the end of this week. This is the real skill: using AI and knowing when you're the one who's right.

questions.q: You throw at 10 m/s. Your friend throws at 20 m/s. His ball goes how many times higher than yours?
questions.hint: Look at your table. Height goes with the square of the speed.
questions.explain: Height ∝ u². Double the speed, 4× the height: 5 m vs 20 m.

questions.q: A stone is thrown straight up at 30 m/s (g = 10). Maximum height?
questions.explain: 900 ÷ 20 = 45 m. That's the cricketer's friend from the hook.

questions.q: Same stone. How long until it's back in the hand?
questions.hint: Time in the air = 2u ÷ g. Up and down take equal time.

questions.q: At the very top of its flight, the ball's velocity and acceleration are...
questions.hint: Watch the sim: the ball stops for an instant, but gravity never switches off.
questions.explain: Velocity is momentarily zero; acceleration stays 10 m/s² downward the whole time. That's why it comes back down.

questions.q: Honest check: this lesson felt mostly like...
options: Interesting, I'd do more of this

lessons.title: What an AI model actually does (it is smaller than you think)
lessons.body:
1 · Hook

ChatGPT does not know anything. It has never read a fact and stored it. It does exactly one thing, billions of times a second, and that one thing is enough to write essays, code, and sometimes confident nonsense.

The one thing: guess the next word. Prove it to yourself below.

2 · Play

This toy is a language model that has read only thirty sentences. Type the start of a sentence and watch what it thinks comes next. Then let it write.

[[widget:nextword]]

Notice: it never "understands". It counts what usually follows what. Scale that up from thirty sentences to most of the internet, from counting to billions of tuned numbers, and you have the thing on your phone.

3 · Name it

Four steps. That is the whole machine.

[[widget:explainer:llm]]

So a language model is a next-token predictor. Text becomes tokens, tokens become numbers, the model predicts the most likely next token, and repeats. It has no database and no fact-checker inside. When it is right, it is because the likely continuation happened to be true. When it is wrong, it sounds exactly as confident. That is called a hallucination.

Why this matters for Class 11: used well, a model is a tireless explainer and practice partner. Used blindly, it hands you wrong answers in perfect English.

4 · Do it

Three quick questions; every one is something you just saw.

5 · AI twist

Ask any AI: "Explain how you work, in three sentences, for a 15-year-old." Compare it with the four steps above. Did it mention predicting the next token? Did it claim to "know" things? Write one line in your diary this week about what it got right and what it fudged.

questions.q: What does a language model fundamentally do?
options: Predicts the next token given the text so far
Stores every fact in a database
questions.hint: Think about step 3 of the explainer.
questions.explain: It predicts the next token, repeatedly. Everything else is built on that.

questions.q: Why can a model state something false with total confidence?
options: It produces likely-sounding text, not verified facts
It was trained only on fiction
questions.hint: Fluent is not the same as true.
questions.explain: It generates the most probable continuation, which can be wrong. Always verify facts.

questions.q: In the toy, after 'chennai is famous for its', why did 'filter' come first?
options: Filter coffee is objectively the best
That pair of words appeared most often in its 30 sentences
questions.explain: The toy counts which word followed which. 'filter' followed 'its' most often in its tiny corpus. Big models do the same with far more data and far more numbers.

options: A chunk of a word or a short word
questions.explain: Tokens are word pieces; 'unbelievable' might be 3 tokens.

lessons.title: Catch the AI out: six lines, three are wrong
lessons.body:
1 · Hook

An AI wrote six confident sentences about India, physics and cricket. Three are false. They all sound equally sure. Can you tell which?

2 · Play

Mark each line True, False, or Can't tell. "Can't tell" is a legitimate answer; it is what a careful person says before checking.

[[widget:spot]]

3 · Name it

What you just practised is called verification, and it is the single most valuable AI skill for the next ten years. The rule is simple: anything you have not checked yourself is a claim, not a fact, no matter how fluent it sounds. Specific numbers, names and dates are the most dangerous, because they look like knowledge.

How to check, in order of effort: does it match something you already know for sure; does a second source (textbook, teacher, a reliable site) say the same; can you test it yourself, like you did with the ball throw.

4 · Do it

Your AI-use diary starts now. This week's three experiments, then write three short paragraphs and submit them as your Friday checkpoint.

  1. Ask an AI to explain the ball-throw lesson a different way. Was anything wrong? How did you check?
  2. Ask it something you already know from Class 10. Did it get it right?
  3. Ask it a fact about your own school or town. Check it. Was it correct?

Submit on the Friday checkpoint page. Two questions below just so this lesson counts as done.

5 · AI twist

Ask the AI: "Are you sure?" after one of its answers. Watch it either defend the answer or suddenly change it. Both tell you something: it has no inner certainty, only text that sounds certain.

questions.q: An AI gives you a very specific date for an event you have never heard of. The right first move is:
options: Treat it as a claim and check a second source
Ask the AI if it is sure, and trust that
questions.hint: Specific is not the same as true.
questions.explain: Specificity is what hallucinations look like. Check a second source.

questions.q: Which is the strongest way to verify a physics claim?
options: Test it yourself, like the ball throw
Search for the same sentence online
questions.hint: You did this in the first lesson.
questions.explain: Testing beats trusting. A second reliable source is next best.

questions.q: A body starts from rest and accelerates at 2 m/s² for 4 s. Final velocity?
A train slows from 30 m/s to 10 m/s over 100 m. Deceleration?
The slope of a velocity–time graph gives...
questions.explain: Slope of v–t is acceleration; area under it is displacement.

questions.q: The area under a velocity–time graph gives...
